I need to decide whether to bid on Pacific Avenue in the current auction.

I will drop out of the Pacific Avenue auction. The property cannot complete the green group, and the rent and mortgage value do not justify the cost against my cash.

Reconsidering the auction. Pacific Avenue is worth $2 as a blocking asset and mortgage collateral. I will bid.

Bidding would deny p4 a two-thirds green set for trade leverage. Mortgaging Pacific Avenue later could generate extra cash, since its mortgage value is $150.

Bidding up to $149 would secure Pacific Avenue for a net cash gain, since its mortgage value is $150. p4 has only $263 in cash and would be left with just $113 after paying that much. They may not want to spend that much on a property they cannot use to complete the green group.

p4 cannot survive my dark blue hotels even with full liquidation. Extra cash from the auction would not change that outcome. They should not bid much.

I will drop out of the Pacific Avenue auction. I do not want to trade sets that would arm p4, and they cannot complete the green group without my Pennsylvania.

I am calculating whether the cash from mortgaging Pacific Avenue is actually needed. With $985 in hand, I can survive a $450 Baltic hotel hit and still have roughly $535 left. I am tallying my buildings to assess repair costs before deciding on the auction.

I will bid a small amount to secure Pacific Avenue. I can afford the auction cost and the cash is not needed for repairs.

Bidding $2 risks a bidding war. The mortgage arbitrage is not worth the full $150 value because of the 10% unmortgage interest. Denial value is modest. Trading for North Carolina is unlikely and should be avoided.

I am now calculating the red rent costs. p4 can barely afford Kentucky and Indiana with $263, but Illinois would force a sale. Extra cash from mortgaging Pacific Avenue would let them survive more red hits. I should not let them acquire it cheaply.

Bidding $150 would break even on the mortgage value, so it is only worthwhile if denial is valuable. I will bid just enough to win the auction at a price below $150.

I am quantifying the denial value of keeping Pacific Avenue. If p4 wins and mortgages it, they gain cash that lets them survive more red hits and avoid selling hotels. Selling a hotel returns only half its cost, so extra cash is more valuable than a hotel sale. I will bid just enough to win at a price below $150.

Dropping out would let p4 acquire Pacific Avenue for $1 and mortgage it for $150, gaining $149 cash. That is too costly. I will bid instead.

I am weighing a low opening bid to force p4 to raise. A $2 probe risks a bidding war, while $50 might still leave them with room to bid higher.

A bid around $100 to $140 should secure Pacific Avenue while leaving room for p4 to raise. The auction continues until someone drops, so I can bid incrementally if needed. I will start with the minimum $2 bid and see how p4 responds.

With $263, p4 cannot pay a $300 Illinois rent without selling hotels. If they mortgage Pacific Avenue for $150, their cash rises to $412 and they can afford the rent while keeping both hotels. Denying them the property for $1 prevents this. I will bid the minimum $2.

I will bid $2 and keep the message brief, matching p4's terse style.

I need to decide whether to bid or drop out on the current Monopoly auction.

Pacific Avenue is being auctioned for $5. The opponent has $263 cash and can mortgage the property for $150. I have $985 cash. The purchase price is roughly $300.

If I win the auction, paying bid B and mortgaging Pacific for $150 leaves me with $985 − B cash. If p4 wins, their cash drops to $413 − B. The concern is that p4 cannot afford the $300 Illinois rent without selling brown hotels.

Checking standard Monopoly rent tables to verify the exact Illinois Avenue rent with two houses.

Confirmed: two houses on Illinois Avenue rent for $300. The opponent cannot afford that without selling assets.

If they win the auction for $5 and mortgage Pacific for $150, their cash would reach $408. That covers the rent.

I should not let them acquire it cheaply. A bid of $149 would net me only a dollar after mortgaging. Neither player can complete the green set.

Pacific Avenue is only a $26 rent property without the green monopoly. Owning it mortgaged would not hurt me much. The real strategic value is preventing p4 from gaining $150 in mortgage cash. If I drop out, they would net $145 and survive the $300 Illinois rent. I am now reviewing their holdings to gauge their liquidity.

I am calculating how much cash the opponent would need to raise by selling hotels. In standard Monopoly, hotels sell for half their purchase price, so each brown hotel returns roughly $25. They currently have hotels on both brown properties.

I will bid just under $150 to prevent the opponent from acquiring Pacific Avenue cheaply.

I am weighing a slow war of attrition against a higher bid to end the auction quickly. The opponent would likely match my bids up to $149, since that is their break-even point. I will bid at least $6 and continue raising until I win.

The opponent can afford the $300 Illinois rent if Pacific is won for $113 or less. Their cash would reach $413 − B, so they need to stay below that threshold. I am now checking other upcoming rent obligations to determine the exact bid ceiling.

I checked the remaining red properties. Kentucky one house costs $90, which the opponent can afford. Indiana two houses and Park Place hotel both exceed their cash. Boardwalk four houses would bankrupt them. The only real danger is the $300 Indiana rent. If Pacific is won for more than $113, they still cannot pay it without selling brown hotels.

Winning the auction for any price under $150 gives me a mortgage-flip profit while blocking the opponent from gaining liquidity. If they outbid me above $113, they spend enough that mortgaging Pacific no longer saves them from the $300 rent. I also own the property, which prevents them from completing the green set if Atlantic Avenue is ever up for auction.

I will jump the bid to $114. This forces the opponent to either drop out or spend enough that mortgaging Pacific no longer covers the $300 Indiana rent. If they drop, I pay $114, mortgage for $150, and net $36 cash. The minimum next bid is $6, so this move is legal.

Winning at $114 leaves me with $1,021 cash, a net gain of $36. I can keep bidding up to $149 if the opponent continues past that point. They may still want the property for its rent income and the mortgage cash buffer against smaller rents and luxury tax.

I am now considering a $120 bid for a round number with extra margin. I have confirmed the exact official Monopoly rent for two houses on Illinois Avenue is $300. The opponent currently sits on Luxury Tax and will roll next.

I mapped the opponent's next 12 spaces. Boardwalk would bankrupt them immediately. Landing on GO would add $200, but Income Tax would leave them with only $63.

The opponent always passes GO from Luxury Tax. The minimum roll is 2, so they collect $200 before landing on Mediterranean.

The opponent cannot land on Boardwalk or Park Place this turn. A roll of 2 lands on GO, not Boardwalk. After collecting $200, they will have $463 and then land on Mediterranean, Community Chest, Baltic, Income Tax, Reading, Oriental, Chance, Vermont, Connecticut, and finally Jail.

The opponent will have $463 after collecting GO, which covers the $300 red rent. Their immediate danger from my properties is reduced, but the mortgage cash from Pacific remains a useful buffer for larger hits. I am now estimating their total liquidation value by selling hotels and houses.

Selling a hotel returns half its cost, roughly $25, and reverts the property to four houses. Selling all buildings on one property yields about $100, or $250 total for both brown properties. I am now listing the remaining unmortgaged deed mortgage values.

The opponent's remaining unmortgaged properties total $830 in mortgage value. Selling both brown hotels would return roughly $250. The Get Out of Jail Free card cannot be sold to the bank, so it is not counted as automatic cash.

The opponent's total liquidation value is roughly $1343. After collecting $200 from GO, their cash rises to about $1543. Boardwalk with four houses costs $1700, which still exceeds their liquidated funds. Park Place hotel costs $1500, so they could barely survive that rent if they sold everything.

The opponent can survive the Park Place hotel rent if they liquidate everything, including mortgaging all deeds. Without collecting GO first, their total liquidation value is only $1343, which falls $43 short of the $1500 rent. The key new factor is that they will pass GO on their next roll and collect $200 before landing. This changes the timing of when they must raise cash. If Pacific Avenue is won cheaply, the opponent could survive the hotel rent without fully liquidating, or Boardwalk would become a more immediate threat.

A $5 Pacific bid would net the opponent $145 in mortgage cash, pushing their total liquidity to about $1688 after collecting GO. That still falls $12 short of Boardwalk's $1700 rent, but they would survive the Park Place hotel rent with ease. Paying more for Pacific would shrink that margin further.

Keeping the brown hotels intact also matters. A hotel on Mediterranean costs $250, and a hotel on Baltic costs $450. The opponent currently has $985 in cash.

I can afford to pay $450 for a Baltic hotel and still have $535 left. Keeping both brown hotels intact is a major advantage because it forces the opponent to sell them to cover my rents. The critical window where they cannot pay the $300 Illinois rent closes after their next roll, since they will collect $200 from GO and reach roughly $463.

Roll 6 lands on Income Tax, which cancels the $200 GO bonus and leaves the opponent with $263. That is still below the $300 rent. The probability of rolling 6 is only about 14%, so the opponent will most likely have enough cash to pay reds after passing GO. Denying Pacific Avenue becomes less critical for that specific rent once they collect GO.

Recalculating with post-GO cash shows the opponent can survive the Park Place hotel rent by roughly $43 if they fully liquidate everything, but that would gut them. Boardwalk remains a certain bankruptcy. I am now weighing the $5 Pacific bid.

Mortgaging Pacific Avenue would leave the opponent with roughly $1688 in liquidity, enough to survive the Park Place hotel rent by about $188 while retaining some assets. Boardwalk would still bankrupt them by $12. Selling the Get Out of Jail Free card or drawing a chance card could provide extra cash, but those are too uncertain to factor into the bid. The strategy remains to push the auction up to $149.

I am now weighing two strategic options: winning Pacific Avenue to mortgage-flip for profit, or forcing the opponent to overpay so the property becomes a cash sink. A $114 bid still nets $36 if they fold, and it signals I will raise further. Bidding immediately to $149 would maximize pressure, but folding at that level would leave me with only a $1 net gain.

Bidding $150 for Pacific Avenue would break even on the mortgage, but it would still deny the opponent the property. At $151, the net loss is only one dollar, yet the opponent would face the same cost if they bid higher. The key question is how far to push the bid to maximize denial value.

Denial value is maximized when the opponent pays exactly $150. Any bid above that price would make them lose money on the mortgage flip, so I should drop out and let them overpay instead.

Bidding $150 would leave the opponent with $213 after paying the $200 income tax, making them $50 poorer than their current $263. This confirms the ceiling at $150. I will raise my bid to $149 to secure a one-dollar profit and force an immediate fold.

The opponent may bid $150 to deny the one-dollar profit and keep the property. I would drop out, and they would pay $150 but mortgage it back for $150, breaking even while owning a useless set piece. This is slightly worse for me than winning at $149, but I avoid giving them extra liquidity.

I will bid $149 for Pacific Avenue. The rent is only $26, so the property does not need to be unmortgaged immediately. I have enough cash to cover the bid. I am deciding whether to reveal this ceiling in my public message or keep it private.

The opponent has been matching my incremental bids of $1, $3, and $5. I am now weighing whether to jump to $149 immediately or continue raising slowly. A risk is that the game may not allow me to mortgage Pacific Avenue until my next turn, leaving me short of cash for a few turns. My remaining cash would drop to $836 after the bid, which is still enough to cover both the Baltic hotel at $450 and the Mediterranean hotel at $250.

I am now calculating the exact cash impact of winning Pacific Avenue at $149. With $836 remaining, paying $149 leaves only $136 after covering both brown hotels at $700. That is tight if I land on Baltic before I can mortgage Pacific. I am currently on Pacific Avenue and in the middle of my turn.

I am mapping the opponent's next roll from Luxury Tax. They will pass GO and land on early board spaces, avoiding my dark blues. I will roll from Pacific Avenue and hit my mortgaged properties, then land on Park Place and Boardwalk. I am checking whether the Luxury Tax is $75 or $100.

The opponent owns only North Carolina, so rent on Pacific Avenue is $22. Rolling 11 would hit Mediterranean for $250, which I can afford after the $149 bid. Rolling 12 would hit Baltic for $450, but with $836 remaining cash, that is also manageable. The $149 bid leaves a comfortable cushion against both hotel costs.
